claim: Some sea slugs sequester chloroplasts from algal food in their intestinal cells and photosynthesize for months.
source: Some sea slugs sequester chloroplasts from algal food in their intestinal cells and photosynthesize for months.
evidence: This is a well-established phenomenon supported by multiple citations in the manuscript and experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The absence of algal nuclei in sacoglossan cells makes kleptoplasty distinct from other symbioses and plastid acquisitions.
source: The absence of algal nuclei in sacoglossan cells makes kleptoplasty distinct from other symbioses and plastid acquisitions (de Vries and Archibald, 2018; Rauch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and electron microscopic studies mentioned in the text.

claim: The Fv/Fm value of PoB starved for 38 days was 0.68-0.69.
source: The Fv/Fm value, which reflects the maximum quantum yield of PSII, was 0.68–0.69 in the 'd38' PoB group (starved for 38 days)
evidence: Direct measurement data from PAM fluorometry experiments.

claim: The Fv/Fm value of PoB starved for 109-110 days was 0.57-0.64.
source: 0.57–0.64 in the 'd109' group (starved for 109–110 days; Figure 2A)
evidence: Direct measurement data from PAM fluorometry experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Healthy Halimeda borneensis showed Fv/Fm values of 0.73-0.76.
source: These values were only slightly lower than those of healthy Halimeda borneensis, a kleptoplast donor of PoB (Maeda et al., 2012), which showed Fv/Fm values of 0.73–0.76.
evidence: Direct measurement data from PAM fluorometry experiments.

claim: PoB kleptoplasts retain a similar photochemical efficiency of PSII to that of the food algae for more than 3 months.
source: The Fv/Fm value suggested that PoB kleptoplasts retain a similar photochemical efficiency of PSII to that of the food algae for more than 3 months.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of Fv/Fm values between starved PoB and healthy algae.

claim: Starved PoB individuals displayed gross photosynthetic oxygen production.
source: Based on the measurement of oxygen concentrations in seawater, starved PoB individuals ('d38' and 'd109') displayed gross photosynthetic oxygen production (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Direct measurement data from oxygen sensor experiments shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The mean longevity of starved PoB was 156 days under continuous darkness.
source: The mean longevity was 156 days under continuous darkness
evidence: Direct measurement data from longevity experiments.

claim: The mean longevity of starved PoB was 195 days under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycle.
source: 195 days under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycle (p=0.022; Figure 2D)
evidence: Direct measurement data from longevity experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Light exposure significantly prolongs PoB longevity.
source: The mean longevity was 156 days under continuous darkness and 195 days under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark cycle (p=0.022; Figure 2D), indicating that light exposure significantly prolongs PoB longevity.
evidence: Statistical analysis of longevity data showing significant difference (p=0.022).

claim: Kleptoplast photosynthesis increases the starvation resistance of PoB.
source: Although future research methods may allow for more experimental analyses of kleptoplast functions, the currently most straightforward idea is that kleptoplast photosynthesis increases the starvation resistance of PoB.
evidence: Inference based on the longevity data and photosynthetic activity measurements.

claim: Two types of circular kpDNA and one whole mitochondrial DNA were obtained from PoB.
source: Illumina sequencing provided two types of circular kpDNA and one whole mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Direct sequencing data from Illumina platform.

claim: The sequenced kpDNAs corresponded to Rhipidosiphon lewmanomontiae and Poropsis spp.
source: The sequenced kpDNAs corresponded to those of the predominant kleptoplast donors of PoB (Maeda et al., 2012), i.e., Rhipidosiphon lewmanomontiae (AP014542; hereafter 'kRhip') and Poropsis spp. (AP014543; hereafter 'kPoro'; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and sequence comparison with known algal species.

claim: PoB kpDNAs contained all the 59 conserved chloroplastic genes in Bryopsidales algae.
source: PoB kpDNAs contained all the 59 conserved chloroplastic genes in Bryopsidales algae (e.g., psbA and rpoA), although they lacked four to five of the dispensable genes (i.e., petL, psb30, rpl32, rpl12, and ccs1; Figure 3C).
evidence: Comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PoB kpDNAs lacked four to five dispensable genes (petL, psb30, rpl32, rpl12, and ccs1).
source: PoB kpDNAs contained all the 59 conserved chloroplastic genes in Bryopsidales algae (e.g., psbA and rpoA), although they lacked four to five of the dispensable genes (i.e., petL, psb30, rpl32, rpl12, and ccs1; Figure 3C).
evidence: Comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A tblastn homology search using A614 obtained no reliable hits against the kpDNA sequences, except for the chlD gene.
source: A tblastn homology search using A614 obtained no reliable hits (E-value < 0.0001) against the kpDNA sequences, except for the chlD gene, which resembled the kpDNA-encoded chlL gene (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis using tblastn with specific E-value threshold.

claim: The PoB genome assembly contained 927.9 Mbp.
source: The genome assembly contained 927.9 Mbp (99.1% of the estimated genome size; 8647 scaffolds; N50 = 1.45 Mbp; 77,230 gene models; Supplementary file 4; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Direct sequencing and assembly data.

claim: The PoB genome assembly had an N50 of 1.45 Mbp.
source: The genome assembly contained 927.9 Mbp (99.1% of the estimated genome size; 8647 scaffolds; N50 = 1.45 Mbp; 77,230 gene models; Supplementary file 4; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Direct sequencing and assembly data.

claim: The PoB genome contained 77,230 gene models.
source: The genome assembly contained 927.9 Mbp (99.1% of the estimated genome size; 8647 scaffolds; N50 = 1.45 Mbp; 77,230 gene models; Supplementary file 4; Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Gene modeling from assembled genome.

claim: BUSCO analysis showed 93% coverage of the eukaryote conserved gene set in the PoB genome.
source: Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) analysis using the eukaryota_odb9 dataset showed high coverage (93%) of the eukaryote conserved gene set, indicating that the gene modeling was sufficiently complete to enable HGT searches (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: BUSCO analysis results indicating genome completeness.

claim: Searches of PoB gene models found no evidence of algae-derived HGT.
source: Searches of PoB gene models found no evidence of algae-derived HGT.
evidence: Multiple bioinformatic analyses including blastp, LCA analysis, and GO annotation found no photosynthetic genes of algal origin.

claim: No PoB gene model was annotated as a gene relating to 'Photosynthesis (GO:0015979)'.
source: In gene function assignment with Gene Ontology (GO) terms, no PoB gene model was annotated as a gene relating 'Photosynthesis (GO:0015979)," although the same method found 72 to 253 photosynthesis-related genes in the five referential algal species (Figure 4A).
evidence: GO annotation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Six PoB genes were assigned to the child terms of 'Plastid (GO:0009536)'.
source: Six PoB genes assigned to the child terms of 'Plastid (GO:0009536)' were found (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: GO annotation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The six PoB genes assigned to plastid-related GO terms had no relationships to photosynthesis.
source: The function of these six genes had no relationships to photosynthesis (Supplementary file 7); six genes relate proteasome (p2972c65.3), arginine kinase (p197c68.18), DNA-binding response regulator (p234c64.89), chromatin structure (p466c59.83), mitochondrial inner membrane translocase (p503c65.126), and functionally unknown protein (p45387c41.1).
evidence: Functional annotation of the six genes showing no photosynthetic function.

claim: The PoB genome contains no algae-derived photosynthetic genes.
source: It was thus concluded that the PoB genome assembly contains no algae-derived photosynthetic genes.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence from various bioinformatic analyses (Exonerate, tblastn, phylogenetic analysis).

claim: 162 DG-up-regulated genes were found in PoB.
source: As a result, 162 DG-up-regulated genes were found (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.01, triplicate samples; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: RNA-Seq differential expression analysis with statistical threshold.

claim: DG-up-regulated genes are enriched for genes involved in proteolysis, carbohydrate metabolism, and immunity.
source: These up-regulated genes are enriched for genes involved in proteolysis (GO terms: 'Proteolysis,' 'Aspartic-type endopeptidase activity,' 'Cysteine-type endopeptidase inhibitor activity', and 'Anatomical structure development'), carbohydrate metabolism ('Carbohydrate metabolic process', 'One-carbon metabolic process', 'Cation binding', and 'Regulation of pH'), and immunity ('Defense response'; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: GO enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: OG0000132 contained 203 cathepsin D-like genes of PoB.
source: The most distinctive orthogroup in the six groups was OG0000132, which contained 203 cathepsin D-like genes of PoB.
evidence: Orthogroup analysis from comparative genomics.

claim: Forty-five of the 203 cathepsin D-like genes were DG-up-regulated.
source: Forty-five of the 203 genes were DG-up-regulated, and Fisher's exact test supported the significant enrichment of DG-up-regulated genes (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 11).
evidence: Statistical analysis of differential expression within orthogroup.

claim: Other heterobranchian mollusks only had four to five genes belonging to OG0000132.
source: Other heterobranchian mollusks only had four to five genes belonging to OG0000132 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The E. marginata genome assembly comprised 14,285 scaffolds containing 791,005,940 bp.
source: The assembly comprised 14,285 scaffolds containing 791,005,940 bp.
evidence: Direct sequencing and assembly data for E. marginata.

claim: The final E. marginata assembly comprised 790.3 Mbp with N50 = 0.23 Mbp and 70,752 genes.
source: Using the same methods as described for PoB, one complete circular kpDNA, one complete mtDNA, and 790.3 Mbp nucDNA (87.8% of the estimated genome size; 14,149 scaffolds; N50 = 0.23 Mbp; 70,752 genes; Supplementary files 1, 4, 13, and 14) were sequenced for E. marginata.
evidence: Direct sequencing and assembly data for E. marginata.

claim: No credible photosynthetic gene was detected from E. marginata nucDNA.
source: No credible photosynthetic gene was detected from E. marginata nucDNA (annotation data; DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.13042016).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of E. marginata genome.

claim: Almost all duplicated PoB cathepsin D-like genes (201/203) belonged to the γ-clade.
source: Almost all duplicated PoB genes (201/203) belonged to the γ-clade, including one E. marginata gene (e8012c40.2).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis of cathepsin D-like genes.

claim: All DG-up-regulated cathepsin D-like DEGs belonged to the γ-clade.
source: Interestingly, all DG-up-regulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) belonged to the γ-clade
evidence: Combined phylogenetic and differential expression analysis.

claim: RELAX suggested that the γ-clade evolved under relaxed selection relative to the rest branches (K = 0.44, p<0.001).
source: The CodeML analysis (branch-site model) determined no significant positive selection on the basal node of the γ-clade (p>0.05, χ2 test), but RELAX suggested that the γ-clade evolved under relaxed selection relative to the rest branches (K = 0.44, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of molecular evolution using RELAX software.

claim: The cathepsin D-like genes formed multiple tandem repeat structures in the PoB genome.
source: The cathepsin D-like genes formed multiple tandem repeat structures in the PoB genome, although other Heterobranchia had no tandem repeat (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Genomic structure analysis shown in Figure 6B and supplements.

claim: PoB gains adaptive photosynthetic activity without acquiring any of the many algal nucleic genes involved in photosynthesis.
source: However, our studies indicate that PoB gains adaptive photosynthetic activity without acquiring any of the many algal nucleic genes involved in photosynthesis.
evidence: Comprehensive genomic analysis showing absence of algal photosynthetic genes combined with demonstration of photosynthetic activity.

claim: This is evidence of a phenotype (and organelle) acquisition, although temporally, from the donor without DNA or RNA transfer.
source: This is evidence of a phenotype (and organelle) acquisition, although temporally, from the donor without DNA or RNA transfer.
evidence: Inference based on the combination of photosynthetic activity and absence of algal genes.

claim: The maintenance of algae-derived protein activity is the most probable mechanism for retaining PoB photosynthesis.
source: The combination of genomics and transcriptomics suggests that the maintenance of algae-derived protein activity is the most probable mechanism for retaining PoB photosynthesis.
evidence: Inference based on absence of algal genes and presence of photosynthetic activity.

claim: Apolipoprotein D-like, cathepsin D-like, and lectin-like genes are candidate KRM genes.
source: Candidate KRM genes, i.e., apolipoprotein D-like, cathepsin D-like, and lectin-like genes, were also identified using a combination of genomic and transcriptomic analysis.
evidence: Combined analysis of gene expansion and differential expression.

claim: The estimated genome size of PoB is 936 Mb.
source: The above procedure was repeated for three PoB individuals, and an estimated genome size of 936 Mb was determined.
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements.

claim: Kleptoplast has never been found in germ cells of sea slug.
source: Kleptoplast has never been found in germ cells of sea slug.
evidence: Statement in Figure 1A caption based on anatomical studies.

claim: A common ancestor of Sacoglossa acquired non-functional chloroplast retention phenomena.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that a common ancestor of Sacoglossa acquired non-functional chloroplast retention phenomena (without the maintenance of photosynthetic function), and multiple sacoglossan groups subsequently acquired the ability to maintain photosynthetic activity.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis cited from Christa et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Multiple sacoglossan groups subsequently acquired the ability to maintain photosynthetic activity.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that a common ancestor of Sacoglossa acquired non-functional chloroplast retention phenomena (without the maintenance of photosynthetic function), and multiple sacoglossan groups subsequently acquired the ability to maintain photosynthetic activity.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis cited from Christa et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The algal nucleus, rather than the plastids, encodes most photosynthetic proteins.
source: Because the algal nucleus, rather than the plastids, encodes most photosynthetic proteins, the mechanism to maintain photosynthetic proteins is especially intriguing, given that photosynthetic proteins have a high turnover rate (de Vries and Archibald, 2018; Pelletreau et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Photosynthetic proteins have a high turnover rate.
source: Because the algal nucleus, rather than the plastids, encodes most photosynthetic proteins, the mechanism to maintain photosynthetic proteins is especially intriguing, given that photosynthetic proteins have a high turnover rate (de Vries and Archibald, 2018; Pelletreau et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Previous PCR-based studies have suggested the HGT of algal nucleic photosynthetic genes to the nucDNA of Elysia chlorotica.
source: Previous polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based studies have suggested the HGT of algal nucleic photosynthetic genes (e.g., psbO) to the nucDNA of the sea slug, Elysia chlorotica (Pierce et al., 1996; Pierce et al., 2009; Pierce et al., 2007; Pierce et al., 2003; Rumpho et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of previous research with multiple citations.

claim: A genomic study of E. chlorotica (N50 = 824 bases) provided no reliable evidence of HGT.
source: A genomic study of E. chlorotica (N50 = 824 bases) provided no reliable evidence of HGT but predicted that fragmented algal DNA and mRNAs contribute to its kleptoplasty (Bhattacharya et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to previous genomic study.

claim: An improved genome of E. chlorotica (N50 = 442 kb) was published recently.
source: Although an improved genome of E. chlorotica (N50 = 442 kb) was published recently, this study made no mention of the presence or absence of algae-derived genes (Cai et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to recent genomic study.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses of other sea slug species failed to detect HGT.
source: Although transcriptomic analyses of other sea slug species failed to detect HGT (Chan et al., 2018; Wägele et al., 2011), transcriptomic data were insufficient to ascertain genomic gene composition (de Vries et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of previous transcriptomic studies with citations.

claim: P. ocellatus is a species complex.
source: However, a recent phylogenetic analysis showed that P. ocellatus is a species complex (a set of closely related species; Figure 1F; Christa et al., 2014c; Krug et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2012; Meyers-Muñoz et al., 2016; Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis from multiple cited studies shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The retention period of photosynthesis differs among sacoglossan species (1 to >300 days).
source: The retention period of photosynthesis differs among sacoglossan species (1 to >300 days; Figure 1B; Christa et al., 2015, Christa et al., 2014a, Christa et al., 2014b; Evertsen et al., 2007; Laetz and Wägele, 2017)
evidence: Summary of retention periods from multiple cited studies.

claim: Electron microscopic studies have indicated that the sea slug maintains photosynthetic activity without algal nuclei.
source: Electron microscopic studies have indicated that the sea slug maintains photosynthetic activity without algal nuclei (Hirose, 2005; Kawaguti, 1965; Laetz and Wägele, 2019; Martin et al., 2015; Pierce and Curtis, 2012).
evidence: Summary of electron microscopy studies with citations.
